description: Η ομάδα μας έχει στόχο την εύρεση γήινων αναλόγων από γεωλογική σκοπιά. Είμαστε ανοικτοί στη διεπιστημονική συνεργασία, σε νέες ιδέες και διαφορετικές οπτικές προσέγγισης του θέματος. Αναζητούμε άτομα με ενθουσιασμό για την πλανητική επιστήμη και με διάθεση για συνεργατικότητα.
summary:
AresBasalt is a mineralogical matching tool developed to identify optimal terrestrial analogues for Martian basaltic regolith, supporting future In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) and extraterrestrial habitat construction.

Using QGIS and Python, we processed calibrated, atmospherically corrected satellite datasets—NASA’s CRISM (MTR3) for Martian sites (such as Jezero and Gale craters) and ESA’s Sentinel-2 (Level-2A) for Earth locations, highlighting Mount Vourinos in Western Macedonia, Greece. By isolating diagnostic spectral bands (including SWIR) and normalizing mineral profiles across four key components—Plagioclase, Pyroxene, Olivine, and Clays/Hydration—our application quantitatively compares Earth and Mars rock compositions, ranks terrestrial matches by similarity, and flags high clay content unsuitable for sintering or 3D printing.

This project is vital because shipping construction materials to Mars is prohibitively expensive. By pinpointing accessible, high-similarity basalt analogues on Earth, AresBasalt enables researchers and engineers to cost-effectively test regolith-based construction technologies before deploying them on the Red Planet.
details:
AresBasalt ("Project Houston, We Have an Analogue!") is a mineralogical matching platform designed to find the closest terrestrial analogues on Earth for Martian basaltic regolith. By comparing remote-sensing mineral profiles across four core basalt components—plagioclase, pyroxene, olivine, and clays/hydration—the application ranks Earth locations by geochemical similarity and evaluates their suitability for In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU), such as regolith sintering and 3D-printed Martian habitats.

To build a reliable cross-planetary baseline, we used QGIS to process calibrated NASA MRO CRISM (MTR3) hyperspectral summary products for Mars (such as Jezero and Gale craters) alongside ESA Sentinel-2 (Level-2A) multispectral summer imagery for Earth, highlighting geological formations in Greece like Mount Vourinos and Mikrothives/Volos. Using the Raster Calculator and targeted spectral band filtering (OLINDEX3, LCPINDEX2/HCPINDEX2, R770, BD1900_2, and SWIR ratios), we masked out non-Martian noise such as vegetation, water, and terrain shadows, then extracted and normalized Zonal Statistics (Mean and Max values) onto a unified 0–100% abundance scale.

On the software side, we developed the application using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Python logic to perform instant multi-dimensional vector comparisons. Instead of processing heavy satellite files on the spot, our algorithm rapidly compares normalized four-mineral vectors, computes similarity percentages, and applies automated engineering rules that flag high clay and hydration content—which can compromise structural integrity during heating and sintering. By decoupling heavy GIS preprocessing from a lightweight, real-time web interface, AresBasalt provides researchers with an accessible, low-cost tool to test Martian construction technologies right here on Earth before deploying them to the Red Planet.
